\chapter{Asking Someone's Name}
\label{ch:asking-a-name}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone's name in either register and say it was a pleasure.}

Asking Someone's Name — the chapter run end to end.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cómo]{cómo — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} your first question word}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-como}



\begin{quote}
To ask someone's name or how they are, you need this word first. \emph{Cómo} — \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} — and hiding inside it is a little Latin word for \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{} that you already own a dozen English versions of.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cómo} — \textquotedblleft{}how.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{quo modo} — not a word but a \textbf{two-word phrase}, \textquotedblleft{}in what \textbf{manner}.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{The two halves, and their English cousins:}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{modo} (\textquotedblleft{}manner, measure\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ English \textbf{mode}, \textbf{modal}, \textbf{model}, \textbf{moderate}, \textbf{modify}, com\textbf{mod}ity.
  \item \emph{quo} (\textquotedblleft{}in what\textquotedblright{}) is the Latin question-stem \textbf{qu-}, the seed of nearly every Spanish question word.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{How the phrase became one word — the wearing-down.} Spanish did not borrow \emph{cómo} ready-made; it \textbf{eroded} out of \emph{quo modo} over centuries of everyday speech. The final \emph{-do} fell off and the middle collapsed:

\begin{quote}
\emph{quomodo} $\to$ \emph{quomo} $\to$ \textbf{como}
\end{quote}

The \emph{qu-} (a \emph{kw} sound) flattened to a plain \emph{k}, written \emph{c} before \emph{o}. What is left is a whole Latin phrase worn smooth — the way a pebble loses its edges in a river. The same erosion gave Italian \emph{come}, Portuguese \emph{como}, French \emph{comme}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cómo\textquotedblright{} — \emph{CÓ-mo}, stress on the first syllable
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cómo\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}mode\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}model\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{modo} root
  \item the erosion — \textquotedblleft{}quo modo, quomo, como\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{cómo} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}How.\textquotedblright{}) Walk the erosion: \emph{quo modo} $\to$ ? $\to$ \emph{cómo}. (\emph{Quomo} $\to$ \emph{como}.) What did the two Latin halves mean? (\emph{Quo}, \textquotedblleft{}in what\textquotedblright{}; \emph{modo}, \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{} — the root of English \emph{mode} and \emph{model}.) Next: the two marks Spanish puts on a question.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿cómo?]{¿cómo? — the two marks that say \textquotedblleft{}this is a question\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-como-acento}



\begin{quote}
You have the word \emph{cómo}. Written down, it wears \textbf{two} marks that English has no equivalent for — and neither of them is decoration. Both do a job English leaves to word order and guesswork.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cómo — the word itself, and where it came from.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — the upside-down opener}
Spanish questions open with an upside-down \textbf{¿} and close with a normal \textbf{?}: \emph{¿cómo?}

Why? Spanish word order often does not change in a question — \emph{cómo estás} looks the same whether you are asking or reporting. A reader coming to a long sentence would not know to raise their pitch until they hit the mark at the very end, by which time it is too late. The \textbf{¿} is a piece of engineering: it tells your voice, in advance, what shape the sentence has. Only the \textbf{question part} gets bracketed, not necessarily the whole line.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the accent that marks a question}]
Now watch the accent mark do real work:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{cómo} & \textquotedblleft{}how?\textquotedblright{} — the question word \\
\textbf{como} & \textquotedblleft{}like / as\textquotedblright{} — or \textquotedblleft{}I eat\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same letters, same sound. The written accent is the \textbf{only} thing marking the difference:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿\textbf{Cómo} estás?} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{How} are you?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{\textbf{Como} tú.} — \textquotedblleft{}Like you.\textquotedblright{} / \emph{Yo \textbf{como}.} — \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Every question word you will meet — \emph{qué, dónde, cuándo, quién} — carries this accent for exactly this reason. It is not about stress (the stress is the same either way); it is a flag that says \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}asking.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿cómo?\textquotedblright{} — with question intonation, opening high
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}cómo\textquotedblright{} (how?) then \textquotedblleft{}como\textquotedblright{} (like / I eat)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Spanish open a question with \textbf{¿}? (Word order often does not change, so the reader needs the warning \textbf{before} the sentence, not after.) What changes when the accent disappears from \emph{cómo}? (It stops being the question word — \emph{como} means \textquotedblleft{}like / as,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{}) Which word asks for a person? (\emph{Quién}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qu-]{The \emph{qu-} question family — one ancient pattern, many clues}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-familia-qu}



\begin{quote}
You traced \emph{cómo} back to Latin \emph{quomodo}. Focus now on its first piece, \emph{qu-}, without trying to use a whole set of new question words yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cómo — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \emph{quomodo}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin used a recurring \emph{qu-} stem in questions. Spanish preserves that family, although centuries of sound change gave the modern forms different shapes:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish clue} & \textbf{$\leftarrow$ Latin} & \textbf{future meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{qué} & \emph{quid} & what \\
\emph{quién} & \emph{quem} & who \\
\emph{cuál} & \emph{qualis} & which \\
\emph{cuándo} & \emph{quando} & when \\
\emph{cuánto} & \emph{quantus} & how much \\
\textbf{cómo} & \emph{quomodo} & how \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

These are previews, not vocabulary to produce today. For now, use the family only as an etymological clue: a question form beginning \emph{qu-} or \emph{cu-} may continue the same Latin pattern. \emph{Dónde}, \textquotedblleft{}where,\textquotedblright{} is an exception from Latin \emph{de unde}, \textquotedblleft{}from where.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the Latin source of \emph{cómo}
  \item the recurring Latin question stem
  \item which word in the family asks for a person
  \item whether the table is today's production list or a preview
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which old stem connects \emph{qué, quién, cuándo,} and \emph{cómo}? (\emph{qu-}.) Which word in the preview is the exception? (\emph{Dónde}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[se llama]{se llama — the reflexive that fits \emph{usted}}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-se-llama}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{me llamo} (\textquotedblleft{}I call myself\textquotedblright{}). To ask someone \emph{else} their name — especially formally, with \emph{usted} — you need the version that loops back on \emph{them}: \emph{se llama}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item me llamo — the reflexive \textquotedblleft{}I call myself.\textquotedblright{}
  \item tú / usted — and the key fact that \emph{usted} takes \emph{he/she} verb forms.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{se llama} = \textbf{se} (\textquotedblleft{}himself / herself / yourself-formal\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{llama} (\textquotedblleft{}calls\textquotedblright{}). So \emph{se llama} = \textquotedblleft{}he/she calls himself,\textquotedblright{} or — because \emph{usted} uses third-person forms — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you} (formal) call yourself.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{se} — the reflexive pronoun for the third person (and for \emph{usted}). Root: Latin \textbf{sē} (\textquotedblleft{}himself, herself, itself\textquotedblright{}). That same \emph{se-} — carrying the sense of \textquotedblleft{}self / apart / aside\textquotedblright{} — is bolted onto a shelf of English words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{se}cede — \emph{se} + \emph{cedere} (\textquotedblleft{}go apart\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{se}clude, \textbf{se}gregate (\textquotedblleft{}apart from the flock\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{se}parate.
  \item \textbf{se}duce — \emph{se} + \emph{ducere} (\textquotedblleft{}lead aside\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{se}cure — \emph{se} + \emph{cura} (\textquotedblleft{}free from care\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{se}cret (\textquotedblleft{}set apart\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

Every one is something turned in on itself or set apart — the same idea as a reflexive looping the action back on the doer.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the reflexive pronoun changes with the person}]
The verb \emph{llamar} stays, but the little reflexive word in front shifts to match \emph{who} is doing the calling:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{me} llamo — \emph{I} call myself
  \item \textbf{te} llamas — \emph{you (informal, tú)} call yourself
  \item \textbf{se} llama — \emph{he / she / you (formal, usted)} calls himself/yourself
\end{itemize}

Three persons, three pronouns: \emph{me / te / se}. That \emph{se} is exactly why the formal \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{} is \emph{¿cómo \textbf{se} llama usted?} — \emph{usted}, born from \textquotedblleft{}your grace,\textquotedblright{} politely takes the \emph{he/she} shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}se llama\textquotedblright{} — \emph{seh YA-ma}
  \item the set — \textquotedblleft{}me llamo, te llamas, se llama\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}se\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}secede\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}seclude\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}separate\textquotedblright{} — the set-apart root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which reflexive goes with \emph{usted} — \emph{te} or \emph{se}? (\emph{se} — because \emph{usted} takes third-person forms.) What's the \textquotedblleft{}self/apart\textquotedblright{} root inside \emph{secede} and \emph{separate}? (Latin \emph{se-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿cómo se llama usted?]{¿cómo se llama usted? — assembling the question, and answering it}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-como-se-llama}



\begin{quote}
Everything you built this chapter clicks into one sentence: how to ask a stranger their name, and how to answer back. This is your first real two-way exchange.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cómo · se llama · usted
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{¿Cómo se llama usted?} = \emph{cómo} (\textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{se llama} (\textquotedblleft{}do you-formal call yourself\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{usted} (\textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} formal).

Literally: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}How do you call yourself?\textquotedblright{}} Spanish asks \emph{how}, not \emph{what}, for a name — you're asking by what name a person goes, the manner they're called.

\textbf{The informal version}, for a friend, swaps the reflexive and drops the formal pronoun: \textbf{¿Cómo te llamas?} (\emph{te llamas}, from \emph{tú}). Same question, two registers — exactly the \emph{tú}/\emph{usted} choice from earlier, now live in a real sentence:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item To a stranger, an elder, a customer $\to$ \emph{¿Cómo se llama usted?}
  \item To a friend, a child, a peer $\to$ \emph{¿Cómo te llamas?}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{How to answer}
You already have the answer from the \emph{me llamo} lesson: \textbf{Me llamo \_\_\_.}

\begin{quote}
— ¿Cómo se llama usted? — \textbf{Me llamo David.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ask a stranger their name — \emph{¿cómo se llama usted?}
  \item ask a friend the same — \emph{¿cómo te llamas?}
  \item the whole mini-exchange — ask, then answer with \emph{me llamo \_\_\_}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Formal vs. informal \textquotedblleft{}what's your name\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{¿Cómo se llama usted?} / \emph{¿Cómo te llamas?}) Does Spanish literally ask \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} is your name? (\textquotedblleft{}How\textquotedblright{} — \emph{cómo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mucho]{mucho — \textquotedblleft{}much,\textquotedblright{} and a sound-change you've already seen}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-mucho}



\begin{quote}
One more word before \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you.\textquotedblright{} \emph{mucho} — \textquotedblleft{}much, a lot\textquotedblright{} — and it hides the same Latin-to-Spanish sound trick you spotted in \emph{noche}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{soft-c} — the \textbf{ch} is the \emph{ch} of \emph{church}: \emph{MOO-cho}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mucho} — \textquotedblleft{}much, a lot.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{multus} (\textquotedblleft{}much, many\textquotedblright{}). The English cousins keep the original \emph{-lt-}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{mult}iple, \textbf{mult}itude, \textbf{mult}iply, \textbf{mult}i-purpose, \textbf{mult}imedia.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The sound-change, again:} Latin \emph{multum} $\to$ Spanish \emph{mucho}. The Latin \textbf{-lt-} softened into Spanish \textbf{-ch-} — the very same move as \emph{noctem $\to$ noche} (\emph{-ct- $\to$ -ch-}, as in the \emph{noche} lesson). Spanish has a habit of melting these consonant clusters into \emph{ch}. So a Spanish \emph{-ch-} word very often points back to a Latin \emph{-ct-} or \emph{-lt-} root — and the English cousin usually preserves it (\emph{noct}urnal, \emph{mult}iple).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mucho\textquotedblright{} — \emph{MOO-cho}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mucho\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}multiple\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}multitude\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{mult-} family
  \item \textquotedblleft{}noche\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}mucho\textquotedblright{} — two words, same \emph{-ch-} from a melted Latin cluster
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{mucho} comes from Latin \emph{multus} — what English words keep the \emph{-lt-}? (multiple, multitude, multiply.) What Latin cluster melted into the \emph{-ch-}? (\emph{-lt-}, like \emph{-ct-} did in \emph{noche}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mucho gusto]{gusto $\to$ mucho gusto — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-gusto}



\begin{quote}
The line you say when you shake someone's hand. First the noun \emph{gusto}, then snap \emph{mucho} onto it, and you've got it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mucho — \textquotedblleft{}much,\textquotedblright{} about to modify \emph{gusto}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el gusto} (masculine) — \textquotedblleft{}taste; pleasure, liking.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{gustus} (\textquotedblleft{}a tasting, a taste\textquotedblright{}). The English cousins:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{gust}atory — to do with the sense of taste.
  \item dis\textbf{gust} — \emph{dis-} (\textquotedblleft{}not, opposite\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{gust}: literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dis}taste.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{gusto} — borrowed whole into English, meaning zest, relish, enjoyment.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
False friend to flag: a \emph{gust} of wind is \textbf{not} related — that one's from Old Norse \emph{gustr}. Same spelling, different root. Resemblance isn't proof.
\end{quote}

\textbf{mucho gusto} = \emph{mucho} (\textquotedblleft{}much\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{gusto} (\textquotedblleft{}pleasure\textquotedblright{}) = literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{}} — short for \textquotedblleft{}it's a great pleasure {[}to meet you{]}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{gusto} is masculine (\emph{el gusto}), and \emph{mucho} is in its plain masculine form to match it: another quiet piece of the agreement you've been building.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spanish greets a new acquaintance by naming the \emph{pleasure} of it — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{} — where English names the \emph{person} (\textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet \textbf{you}\textquotedblright{}). The phrase works by itself, so this first exchange needs no extra reply formula.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gusto\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}gusto\textquotedblright{} (English), \textquotedblleft{}disgust\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}gustatory\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mucho gusto\textquotedblright{} — on meeting someone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{mucho gusto} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Much pleasure.\textquotedblright{}) Is \emph{el gusto} masculine or feminine? (Masculine.) And the English cousin of \emph{gusto} built from \emph{dis-}? (\emph{Disgust} — \textquotedblleft{}distaste.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — introducing yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
Ten lessons of atoms now assemble into a real conversation. No new words — just the exchange, run both formally and informally until the \emph{tú} / \emph{usted} choice is automatic.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\textbf{Formal} (a stranger, an elder, a customer):

\begin{quote}
— Buenos días. Me llamo Susana. \textbf{¿Cómo se llama usted?} — Me llamo David. \textbf{Mucho gusto.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Informal} (a friend, a peer): only two words change, and they're the ones that carry the whole social difference:

\begin{quote}
— ¡Hola! Me llamo Susana. \textbf{¿Cómo te llamas?} — Me llamo David. Mucho gusto.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{me llamo} — introduce yourself (\textquotedblleft{}I call myself\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{tú / usted} — the informal vs. formal \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{why} (the retired \emph{thou}; \emph{usted} from \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{¿cómo te llamas? / ¿cómo se llama usted?} — ask a name, in either register, the pronoun (\emph{te} / \emph{se}) tracking the choice.
  \item \textbf{mucho gusto} — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure,\textquotedblright{} pleased to meet you.
\end{itemize}

And one from two chapters back, because it is worth keeping warm: \emph{buenos días} but \emph{buenas tardes} — the describing word copies its noun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full \emph{formal} exchange, both parts
  \item the same exchange \emph{informally} — catch yourself on \emph{se llama} $\to$ \emph{te llamas}
  \item for a police officer, then your best friend — which \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} for each, and why?
  \item point to either speaker and ask \textbf{¿Quién?} — answer with the name
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run the formal version start to finish without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words change between the formal and informal introduction? (\emph{se llama usted} $\to$ \emph{te llamas}.) Next chapter, you will learn how to ask how someone is doing.
\end{tcolorbox}
